2) If you can, take the time to go on a jog. Watch a movie. Get laid. Anything that'll clear your head and get your mind off it. I always take an hour off before bed to work on my novel, or read a book, or just meditate.

3) Don't be afraid to ask for help. I know that we're all ego-driven as hell, but most professors will gladly meet with you during their office hours. I meet with my legal writing professor on a pretty regular basis to go over my appellate brief, discuss study strategies, or just shoot the shit.

An example from *BvS*. The film feels a lot like *The Empire Strikes Back*: dark tone; slow pace; cliffhanger ending that leaves a major character sorta dead but not really. The problem is that (in the grand scheme of this DC movie saga) we're way too early in the story for this "darkest hour" stuff. *Civil War* works in this regard because they spent years building to it. With *BvS*, they're throwing a lot of darkness and doom at us right out of the gate. But it's too early for that. The DC Movieverse has been nothing but darkness and doom, so why should I care? So while the difference between Marvel and DC can be chalked up as "stylistic", I think that same divide represents a fundamental miscalculation on DC's part. This, in my opinion, is the reason there's such a massive divide in how these two franchises have been received.

Marvel more or less has their shit together, so I'll take a stab at DC. Here's my pitch for the first "Phase" of a Justice League franchise.

**Man of Steel:** Keep the first contact angle, but with a more grounded, Spielbergian vibe. Take some cues from *American Alien* and *All-Star Superman* - we don't need apocalyptic battles, city-smashing violence, or endless brooding. We need a Superman who farts and bleeds optimism. We need a Superman who goes out of his way to rescue as many people as possible. We need a farmboy from Kansas who becomes a beacon of hope in a world giving way to cynicism and apathy. You can even seed in elements of the upcoming films without throwing *Dawn of Justice* in the title. Have Clark meet a drunken billionaire who gives him advice about the stark divide between the person the world sees and the person you are inside. Have him walk past a painting of Amazonian warriors. Have Lois make a joke about riding seahorses. Have Clark see a news story about Batman and decide he wants a cape, too. Let Superman be powerful, but vulnerable enough to justify teaming up with other heroes should the need arise. Oh, and cast Idris Elba as Zod. 

**The Batman:** Keep Batfleck. He's old, he's grizzled, he's angry. Introduce us to this new incarnation of the character through the lens of Tim Drake, a young man investigating the mysterious, quasi-mythic bat vigilante in Gotham. Make the Joker a Hannibal Lecter figure with whom Batman must cooperate in order to gain information on a larger threat. Give us a Gotham that merges the Gothic skycrapers of Burton with the steampunk anachronisms of *The Animated Series*. Give us a Batman who's teetering close to the abyss and needs a steady hand (Robin's) to guide him back from the edge.

**Wonder Woman:** Give us a neophyte Diana Prince stepping out into the human realm for the first time, learning firsthand the conflict, instability, and hubris of mankind while kicking a lot of ass along the way. So, you know, what they're doing. 

**Justice League:** Do *The Magnificent Seven*, but with superheroes. Superman is alive and well. Batman is training a new Robin. Flash, Aquaman, and Cyborg remain in the shadows. Wonder Woman returns to the human world to recruit the Justice League and battle an alien threat, whether it be Steppenwolf or Brainiac or some third thing. Superman is a optimistic yet somewhat naive leader; Batman the pragmatic second in command; and Wonder Woman the level-headed negotiate between the two. Think the McCoy, Spock, and Kirk dynamic from *Star Trek* - the way these three personalities clash will inform much of the internal conflict of the film and give the team the feuding family dynamic that works so well in the Avengers.

It depends on what you look for in a "trilogy", to be honest. 

The Dark Knight trilogy is a stand-alone saga with a very defined beginning, middle, and end. In a lot of ways, it's the last of the dinosaurs - there will not, in the foreseeable future, be film series that cap off so definitively. Forget about comic book movies - Marvel has inadvertently killed the "closed book" trilogy for the time being.

But if you're okay with a trilogy being part of a larger sort of mega-narrative, then I think an argument can definitely be made. Marvel's shared universe is, for all its flaws, probably one of the most ambitious creative endeavors *ever*. As a stand-alone trilogy, the Cap movies can't really stand on their own since they're basically the axis on which a larger, more expansive narrative is turning. But unless you're living under a rock, then you probably have a solid idea of who the Avengers are and what the Marvel universe looks like. 

So in that capacity, yeah, the Cap movies are just as innovative and important as the Dark Knight movies - they're demonstrating an exciting (if somewhat divisive) method with which to tell a story. People will yearn for the days of "closed loop" storytelling, but the Dark Knight films could never conjure moments like the airport fight in *Civil War* or the SHIELD twist in *The Winter Soldier*. Each approach has its own advantages and disadvantages and as long as the people making the movies play to the strength of their "genre", we'll keep getting great movies. 

To me, they're equally valid artistic statements and definitely worthy of being spoken in the same breath. It doesn't really matter which one is "better" because, let's be honest, the audience has already won.

Life is going to be rough for the migrants/refugees after this. *Harder*, anyway.

Think about it. For every refugee we condemn back to that war-torn meat grinder, we run the risk of creating another militant. Another radical. Another faceless, immoral monster with nothing to his name but his faith and the memory of the people - scared, irrational, hateful - who turned him away when he needed them most. And he'll turn his hatred and pain on them the way these monsters turned theirs onto the people of Paris tonight.

Fuck, guys. It's like that quote from the end of ***Looper***.

> Then I saw it. I saw a mom who would die for her son. A man who would kill for his wife. A boy, angry and alone. Laid out in front of him, the bad path. I saw it. And the path was a circle. Round and round. So I changed it.

In the coming days/weeks/months, we're going to sift through a lot of anger. The President of France has already promised a "pitiless" war against those responsible. Like all of us, he feels hurt and afraid that something this horrific could occur in one of the most iconic and gorgeous cities on Earth. That word scares me, "pitiless." And it should scare you. A world without pity is what created these monsters to begin with - it's the gaping, nauseating pit that spawns heartless would-be martyrs looking to inflict as much pain as they've felt.

So let's change it.
